title: Slope Grade Calculator: Rise, Run and Percent
description: Relate elevation change and run distance to grade with the Slope Grade Calculator — sampled elevations along your path, percent out. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a path that climbs 60 metres over a 1,000-metre run works out to a 6% grade — the steepness of a serious mountain road, read straight off the elevation change.

Rise 60 m over a 1,000 m run: 60 ÷ 1,000 = 6.0% grade, an angle of 3.43°. Six percent is the figure often cited as a design ceiling for interstate highways in mountainous terrain — sustained, it works engines and brakes hard.

popular_table.note: A 100% grade is 45 degrees, not vertical — a wall is an infinite grade. Percent answers 'how much rise per hundred of run', nothing more mystical.

faq: What is the difference between grade and slope angle?
Grade is the ratio rise ÷ run, expressed as a percent. Slope angle is the geometric angle of the surface in degrees. They describe the same hill in different units — 10% grade is 5.71°, not 10°.
How steep is too steep for a road vehicle?
Ordinary cars manage short 15–20% grades; sustained highway grades are usually designed under about 6%. The steepest public streets in San Francisco exceed 30% — possible, but not a design goal.
Does the calculator use map distance or road distance?
Grade needs the horizontal run. If you enter road distance (measured along the slope), the answer comes out slightly low on steep ground — the Slope Length Calculator separates the two distances.
Yes — any slope steeper than 45° has a grade above 100%, because the rise exceeds the run. Ski-slope pitches and roofs live up there; roads sensibly do not.
What grade do wheelchair ramps use?
Accessibility standards in the US cap ramp running slope at 1:12 (about 8.33%) — a figure worth checking against current local code before building, since this page does arithmetic, not compliance.
Why does my GPS app show a different grade?
Apps average elevation change over different windows and filter GPS noise differently. Short windows exaggerate, long windows smooth — the method matters more than the device.
By convention, descents are often written as negative grades (−6%) or just called a 6% downgrade. The steepness is the same; the sign records direction.
What run should I measure for a whole climb?
Total rise over total run gives the average grade — useful for effort, blind to the steep ramp hiding in the middle. Segment the climb when the steepest part is what matters.
